title: System Design Quick Reference
description: Find a short meaning, a useful rule, and the cost of a design choice. Open the linked lesson for its full walkthrough and example.

entries.name: Begin with the goal
entries.summary: Plan a small school library service. Name the users, their main task, the data, and a clear goal before choosing any tools.
notes: Start with users, tasks, data, and measurable goals. Add parts only when a requirement or a test gives a reason.

entries.name: Requirements and tradeoffs
entries.summary: Separate actions from quality goals. Compare two library plans, keep the rules that must hold, and write down a useful tradeoff.
notes: Separate functional requirements, quality goals, constraints, and data rules before comparing designs.

entries.name: Follow one request
entries.summary: Trace a book search from a browser to a service and database, then follow the reply back. Find where a slow step adds waiting time.
notes: Trace validation, data access, and the complete response. Distinguish empty results from unavailable parts.

entries.name: Estimate demand
entries.summary: Estimate searches per day and per second using simple numbers. Compare an average with a busy period and leave room for uncertainty.
notes: requests per second = requests / seconds. State assumptions and estimate busy periods separately from daily averages.

entries.name: Latency and throughput
entries.summary: Measure how long one request takes and how much work finishes. Use a small p95 example to notice slow replies that an average can hide.
notes: Latency measures one request's elapsed time; throughput counts completed work per period. p95 is not the maximum or a future guarantee.

entries.name: APIs and contracts
entries.summary: Design a small book-search API with clear inputs, replies, limits, and errors. Learn why both sides need the same contract.
notes: An API contract includes inputs, outputs, limits, errors, paging order, and compatibility rules. Empty searches can return a successful empty list.

entries.name: Choose the data
entries.summary: Separate a book title from its physical copies. Use stable IDs and links to keep the library facts clear without repeating every detail.
notes: Separate entities such as Book, Copy, and Loan. Stable IDs connect records; changing titles and shelves should not change identity.

entries.name: SQL and NoSQL choices
entries.summary: Compare tables, documents, and key-value storage using library tasks. Choose by needed reads, writes, and rules instead of a label.
notes: Compare actual database features against queries and correctness rules. SQL/NoSQL labels alone do not determine transactions, speed, or scale.

entries.name: Indexes help find records
entries.summary: Use a book index to understand database indexes. Create a small SQLite title index and learn why faster reads can cost space and write work.
notes: Use indexes for known query patterns. They consume space and add write work; inspect query plans and measure realistic workloads.

entries.name: Transactions and safe updates
entries.summary: Keep a book-copy claim and its loan record together. Use a small SQLite transaction and conditional update to prevent a second claim.
notes: Claim with a conditional write, check whether it succeeded, and keep the claim plus related data in one short transaction. Roll back on error.

entries.name: Scaling up and out
entries.summary: Compare one bigger server with several smaller servers. Use a tiny capacity model, then check the shared parts that may still slow the service.
notes: Scale up adds power to one machine; scale out adds machines.
Capacity estimates depend on workload and shared bottlenecks.
Keep spare room for failures and startup delays.

entries.name: Load balancers
entries.summary: Send requests across healthy servers with a load balancer. Trace round-robin routing and see why shared state and useful health checks matter.
notes: Route only to servers considered ready, with a fallback for no ready targets.
Health checks do not guarantee future request success.
Round robin balances counts, not necessarily work.

entries.name: Caches keep useful copies
entries.summary: Save a copy of a repeated answer in a cache. Trace a hit, a miss, and expiry, then decide which data can safely be a little old.
notes: A cache is a copy, not the official record.
TTL expiry does not promise immediate freshness.
Plan invalidation, key isolation, misses, and cache failure.

entries.name: CDNs and static files
entries.summary: Use a content delivery network to bring public files closer to readers. Plan cache headers, versioned names, and safe rules for private responses.
notes: A CDN edge can cache an origin's public files closer to readers.
Cache headers and cache keys control reuse.
Versioned files still need page-update and old-link plans.

entries.name: Copies improve availability
entries.summary: Use replicas to keep extra data copies, then trace a delayed update and a failed leader. Learn why replicas still need backups and safe failover.
notes: Replicas copy changes; asynchronous replicas can lag.
Failover needs a safe leader decision and routing plan.
Use tested backups to recover from bad changes.

entries.name: Partitioning data
entries.summary: Split records across shards using a clear key. Trace a simple remainder rule, then check hot keys, cross-shard work, and the cost of moving data.
notes: Choose a partition key based on data and access patterns.
Partitioning splits data; replication copies it.
Plan hot keys, cross-shard work, and migrations.

entries.name: Consistency describes agreement
entries.summary: Compare fresh and delayed reads across copies. Use a book checkout to explain consistency promises and the choices made during a network break.
notes: State the exact read/write guarantee required by each action.
Eventual consistency alone gives no fixed convergence deadline.
During partitions, strict agreement may require refusing some work.

entries.name: Queues handle work later
entries.summary: Put slow jobs in a queue and let workers finish them later. Count a growing backlog, then plan acknowledgments, duplicate jobs, and failure handling.
notes: A queue stores waiting work; sustained overload still grows the backlog.
At-least-once delivery can repeat a job.
Acknowledge after safe completion and monitor old or failed jobs.

entries.name: Retries need safe rules
entries.summary: Retry a temporary failure with limits and increasing delays. Use stable request IDs so a lost reply does not repeat an important action.
notes: A lost reply leaves the outcome uncertain.
Use limited attempts, backoff, jitter, and an overall deadline.
A durable idempotency design must protect the effect and record atomically.

entries.name: Timeouts and circuit breakers
entries.summary: Limit waiting with timeouts and pause calls to a failing service with a circuit breaker. Trace closed, open, and half-open states using a small model.
notes: Timeouts limit one wait; deadlines limit the whole job.
Closed allows calls, open blocks them, and half-open tests recovery.
A timeout does not prove the remote write was canceled.

entries.name: Rate limits and backpressure
entries.summary: Keep a busy service from taking too much work. Compare a request limit with a signal to slow down, then trace a small JavaScript model.
notes: Define who and what each limit counts.
Bound queues by size and waiting time.
Coordinate counters when several servers enforce one limit.

entries.name: Backups and recovery
entries.summary: Plan how to recover lost data. Tell backups from replicas, set simple recovery targets, and practise restoring a safe copy.
notes: A replica may copy an accidental deletion.
Measure both lost changes and recovery time.
Restore a backup in a safe practice environment and check its records.

entries.name: Observe and review the design
entries.summary: Use metrics, logs, and traces to understand a service. Check a small error-rate calculation, then review a design with clear evidence.
notes: Show traffic, error rates, latency, and capacity together.
Label the time window and which requests are included.
Avoid secret or unnecessary personal data in logs.

entries.name: Security and privacy in a design
entries.summary: Protect private facts at each boundary. Learn identity checks, permissions, safe inputs, and why a design should collect only the data it needs.
notes: Authentication checks identity; authorization checks permission.
Treat input crossing a boundary as untrusted.
Keep service secrets out of browser code and public repositories.

entries.name: One app or several services?
entries.summary: Compare one application with several services. Keep clear module boundaries, then decide when a separate service is worth its extra work.
notes: A monolith can have clear, well-tested modules.
Service boundaries add network and data coordination work.
Split to meet a measured need, not a diagram-size target.

entries.name: Design a school library service
entries.summary: Plan book search, borrowing, and returns for a small library. Follow one safe loan and explain what happens when two readers want the same copy.
notes: Use a separate ID for each physical copy.
Protect borrow and return rules in database transactions.
Treat cached availability as a hint, not permission to lend.

entries.name: Design a URL shortener
entries.summary: Plan a service that turns a long web address into a short link. Handle code collisions, redirects, expired links, and unsafe destinations.
notes: Enforce code uniqueness in storage.
A redirect need not fetch the destination page.
Plan expiry, blocked links, cache rules, and abuse reports.

entries.name: Design a small chat app
entries.summary: Plan saved messages and live delivery for a small chat. Handle repeated sends, missing connections, message order, and private group access.
notes: A WebSocket carries live updates; storage keeps history.
Use stable IDs for retries and removing repeated deliveries.
Distinguish saved, delivered, and read acknowledgements.

entries.name: Design a news feed
entries.summary: Build a small feed of recent posts. Compare making the feed when it is read with preparing it when a post is written, and protect private posts.
notes: Build on read keeps writes simple; build on write shifts work to fan-out.
A time-and-ID cursor gives stable ordering for paging.
Recheck current permissions for cached feed candidates.

entries.name: Design a file-upload service
entries.summary: Plan a private file upload without sending large files through every app server. Track upload states, check the stored bytes, and clean up failed work.
notes: Store bytes separately from file metadata.
A temporary upload grant must have a narrow key, operation, and lifetime.
Check and serve the same immutable bytes; clean up abandoned uploads.
